text: The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains all colors of the visible spectrum, and when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light—blue and violet—much more strongly than longer wavelengths like red and orange (in fact, scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength). Although violet light is scattered even more than blue, our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and some violet is absorbed in the upper atmosphere, so the sky appears blue to us. Near sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere, so the blue light is scattered away before reaching our eyes, leaving the reds and oranges we see at those times.
